notes.1a: All that was required for a correct answer to this question was identification of the two relevant factors of production from the extract: labour (workers) and capital. No further explanation was necessary. Land is a factor of production and was given as an answer by many candidates, but this was not a correct answer here because it was not specifically indicated in the extract.
notes.1b: Most candidates could identify two reasons why firms merge. Not all then proceeded to develop their answers with explanations however, and it is important to say how, for example, economies of scale can be achieved through lower average costs.
notes.1ci: A large majority of candidates were able to produce the correct answer of an 80 per cent decrease in the number of firms by using the information in the extract.
notes.1cii: This question was correctly answered by most candidates, although many made it very difficult for themselves by working in large numbers of zeroes. When a question is in billions it is much easier to keep billions as working units rather than using 1 000 000 000. The correct answer had 12 zeroes when calculated this way and some candidates lost marks because they counted the zeroes incorrectly. It is also important to remember the currency units in answers, in this case yuan, for full marks to be achieved.
notes.1d: A surprising number of candidates made no attempt at this question, a possible indication that they were either uncomfortable with production possibility curves (PPC) or that they had no knowledge of them. Good candidates however could indicate on a diagram how switching resources from cigarettes to other products involves an opportunity cost which involves a movement along the PPc. Weaker candidates on the other hand incorrectly attempted to either draw demand and supply diagrams or to use price theory to answer this question.
notes.1e: Many candidates did not have a clear understanding of the nature of the Human Development Index (HDI) and were therefore at a great disadvantage when answering this question. HDI is a combination of three measurements: an income index, a life expectancy index, and an education index. It therefore covers more than the more commonly used measurement of living standards, GDP per capita. HDI however is also limited in scope because it does not take into account such aspects of living standards as income distribution and levels of pollution, and examples such as these should have been the focus for the second part of the discussion: why countries with a high HDI might not enjoy a high standard of living.
notes.1f: Answers to this question were generally comprehensive and accurate. Most candidates were able to demonstrate a good understanding of the underlying economic concepts behind the diagram by explaining clearly that the information campaign had led to an increase in demand for fruit, a rise in price and an increase in quantity consumed. As indicated in the general comments above however, there was no requirement to reproduce the diagram given on the question paper.
notes.1g: It was encouraging to see ‘two-sided’ arguments given in the majority of answers to this question. Good answers used the concept of inelastic demand to explain both the limited effect of taxes on consumption of cigarettes and the positive effect on government tax revenues. There was also good understanding of the external costs involved in smoking such as air pollution and costs to healthcare providers.
notes.2a: Almost every candidate gave a correct answer to this question and it was encouraging to see the concept of equilibrium price so well understood.
notes.2b: There were some excellent answers given to this question but, as with Q1(b) , there was also a considerable number of candidates who did not develop their answers sufficiently with explanations. So, for example, job satisfaction was frequently given as a reason but the reason for this job satisfaction was not given as further development to gain a second mark.
notes.2c: It was pleasing to see good understanding of productivity and efficiency demonstrated in answers to this question. This was the key to a comprehensive answer, and the idea could then be developed to analyse reasons for this improved efficiency, such as time saved, fewer mistakes and falling capital costs. Weaker answers however did not did not distinguish between the total costs and the average costs specified in the question. It is not necessary for total costs to fall in order to reduce average costs – in this case that depends on the number of workers employed.
notes.2d: Good candidates were able to see ‘both sides’ of this discussion and evaluate how, for example, monopolies could take advantage of economies of scale in order to reduce average costs and thus reduce prices to consumers. Too many candidates however started from the assumption that there are no benefits to the consumer from monopoly, and were therefore limited to a maximum 5 marks for a ‘one-sided’ answer. It was also important for candidates to understand that the question referred to consumers and that answers which discussed benefits to the firm or its employees could gain no reward.
notes.3a: Answers to this question were good on the whole, with a majority of candidates able to define perfect competition satisfactorily. On the other hand there were some candidates who demonstrated a considerable amount of confusion about perfect competition. It is important to understand that despite being in a competitive market, firms in perfect competition produce identical and not differentiated products and do not try to undercut other firms’ prices. They are unable to do so because they each have only a very small fraction of the total market.
notes.3b: This question proved problematic for those candidates who described the size of firms rather than explaining the influences upon the size. In particular, it was common to see ‘number of employees’ given as an explanatory factor but this is simply one measurement of a firm’s size. Good candidates understood this distinction and explained that the size of the market or the goals of the entrepreneurs would determine the size of the firm, and therefore the number of employees it has.
notes.3c: The most popular approach to answering this question was to analyse the effect of training upon labour productivity, and this was also the most successful approach. It was important however to note that six marks were available and weaker candidates were unable to develop their answers sufficiently. Those who did look at other issues were able to produce excellent answers which analysed motivational factors such as higher wages and improved working conditions.
notes.3d: Having produced competent answers to the first three parts of this question, many candidates then found this section provided too many obstacles for a successful answer. There were very few answers which provided a sound discussion of both sides of the argument and unfortunately many candidates resorted to pre-prepared answers on types of protection. There was also a tendency to ignore the focus of the question - higher economic growth. Some answers which focused on employment or good international relations missed the point. It was rare to see a discussion of the benefits of specialisation and competition, but those who did adopt this approach tended to score highly.
notes.4a: Most candidates could name either the CPI or the RPI as a measure of a country’s inflation rate. Some candidates however were determined to give a long explanation (sometimes with numerical tables) of how this was calculated in terms of a basket of goods and weights, thus wasting time which could have been spent answering other questions.
notes.4b: As with other part (b) questions, the main problem here was a tendency to identify but not explain. Most candidates could identify two reasons for conserving resources such as scarcity and the need to protect them for future use, but scarcity needs to be explained in terms of the economic problem, and future use needs to be explained in terms of output, income or employment.
notes.4c: There was some confusion in the distinction between taxes and subsidies here, but most candidates were able to produce an answer analysing the issue of living standards. The main weakness was a tendency to assume that the subsidies would go straight to poorer consumers without explaining the involvement of the farmers to whom the subsidies were given. It was perfectly acceptable to approach this question from the aspect of farmers’ living standards but difficult to score the full six marks without reference to the living standards of the wider population.
notes.4d: The most successful approach to this question was to structure the answer according to the types of tax and their effects. Thus income tax could be evaluated by its effects on expenditure and incentives to work, whilst corporation tax could be evaluated with regard to its effects on costs of production and incentives to produce. Most candidates concentrated on income tax however, and it was rare to see an answer which covered corporation tax. Unfortunately a significant minority confused direct and indirect taxes, assuming that direct taxes would be added to prices. Needless to say, this approach was unsuccessful.
notes.5a: Most candidates were able to demonstrate a clear understanding of a subsidy.
notes.5b: Whilst an increase in the price of oil does not strictly cause a decrease in the demand for oil, because it causes a movement along the demand curve rather than a shift of the demand curve, an increase in oil price was acceptable as an answer here. This is because the distinction is very subtle and easy for candidates to miss, especially when given in English as a second language. Large numbers of candidates did give an increase in oil price as a cause and so the decision to accept this answer proved justified. Candidates still needed to provide causes which shifted the demand curve to the right however, and there were some good answers which examined the introduction of electric cars and the fall in the price of other fuels.
notes.5c: Most candidates were able to satisfactorily outline the sorts of advantages available to a sole trader. As outlined in the key messages above however, it was common to see disadvantages, such as unlimited liability, also given as answers when not required. Analysis questions such as this one do not require the alternative view to be given – it is not the same as a part (d) Discuss question when two/both sides are required – and here candidates needed to stick closely to the advantages alone. There was also some confusion about the nature of sole trading, with some responses indicating that he/she would be the only employee. This is incorrect because sole traders frequently employ staff to assist them – it is the ownership which is singular.
notes.5d: As was the case with Question 3 , it would have benefitted many candidates to look closely at this part of the question before tackling parts (a) , (b) and (c) . Those who had found these first three parts straightforward often struggled badly with this section because they had a weak understanding of the current account of the balance of payments. The worst examples of this were those candidates who confused deficits on the current account of the balance of payments with budget deficits (government spending exceeding tax revenues), and this led to answers which could not possibly score marks. Even those who correctly identified the deficit as imports exceeding exports often struggled to develop their answer further, and it was rare to see evaluation of the effects of a current account deficit on output, prices and employment. It was even rarer to see ‘the other side’ of the argument satisfactorily developed in terms of the effect of a deficit upon the exchange rate and hence the potential of falling export prices/rising import prices to improve the current account position.
notes.6a: Answers to this question were of a mixed standard and there was some confusion about the nature of unemployment. It was common to see answers which suggested that high unemployment would cause problems for firms due to a shortage of workers, but this is incorrect because the unemployed are a potential source of labour. Unemployment does, however, cause problems for firms because of lack of demand for their products because consumers have less disposable income.
notes.6b: The key to a good answer to this question was to split the two causes of deflation into demand and supply factors. Candidates who did this found it a straightforward task to explain how lack of total demand would put downward pressure on prices and how an increase in total supply would enable firms to lower their prices. Understanding of deflation however was weak on the whole, and a number of candidates confused it with disinflation (a fall in the inflation rate) and even with inflation, which could be an indication that a closer reading of the question was called for.
notes.6c: There were some excellent answers to this question which demonstrated a sound understanding of the implications of very high inflation. There was a considerable amount of confusion of cause and effect regarding very high inflation, and to simply state that inflation causes unemployment is unsatisfactory. High unemployment is usually associated with low levels of inflation, even sometimes with deflation, and this is caused by a lack of demand in the economy. It is possible that unemployment could be caused by higher costs to firms (cost-push inflation) but this needed to be clearly explained in order for marks to be awarded. One of the most effective ways to answer this question was to examine the international trade aspect but few candidates used this approach to show that high inflation reduces a country’s competitiveness, devalues the currency, and reduces the value of exports, whilst improving the competitiveness of imported products.
notes.6d: In contrast to the other parts of this question, answers here usually demonstrated a good understanding of inflation and how increased government spending on training could potentially reduce inflation by improving skills, raising productivity and reducing production costs. The alternative aspect of this discussion however proved much more difficult for many candidates who struggled to find reasons why increased spending on training might not reduce inflation. The most successful approach to this ‘other side’ of the question was to link increased government spending to higher total demand in the economy, which then caused demand-pull inflation.
notes.7a: Most candidates could score one mark by some identification of the ways in which the poor spend less and the rich spend more, but few appreciated the importance of proportions or percentage spending in order to score two marks. It is incorrect to say that the poor spend more on necessities than the rich because recognition needs to be made of the much larger incomes of the rich. So the appropriate answer is to say that the poor spend a higher percentage of their income on necessities and this avoids confusion with absolute amounts of income.
notes.7b: This question was answered well on the whole, with most candidates able to identify that the poor are less likely to be able to repay loans. As with other part (b) questions however, many candidates then failed to develop their answers any further with an appropriate explanation – in this case they are less likely to be able repay because of their smaller income.
notes.7c: There were many problems evident in answers to this question, most notably a lack of understanding about the composition of the labour force. The labour force consists of both the employed and the unemployed, and answers which assumed that the unemployed were excluded from the labour force inevitably produced inappropriate answers. The important aspect of this question was for candidates to consider various possibilities – for example if the extra labour force is not employed by firms then unemployment will increase, but if the extra workers are employed then more goods and services can be produced and economic growth occurs. When a question asks for the effects upon an economy it is a good idea for candidates to structure their answers according to key economic objectives and so the best answers considered how an increase in the labour force could affect economic growth, inflation and unemployment.
notes.7d: This question produced the best ‘two-sided’ answers on the examination paper. The biggest weakness displayed by some candidates was a tendency to air their prejudices about the behaviour of poor people, but overall there were some very good discussions of the potential or otherwise of reducing poverty by providing loans to the poor. The best answers examined how the loans could be spent on education which would provide job opportunities and income, along with the possibility of starting businesses which would also provide incomes to the poor. This was then contrasted with the potential problems caused when the loans were spent on unsuitable items, and the difficulties the poor might face repaying the loans and the interest, thus increasing their financial problems
